parts.label: d
parts.display_text: Stable neon-22 has roughly equal numbers of protons and neutrons. The much larger stable gold-197 nucleus has many more neutrons than protons. Explain why stable heavy nuclei need a higher neutron-to-proton ratio.

sup-0f80619981b08d20-w13:a.i.hint: Keep the proton count, neutron count and total nucleon count separate.
notes: Isotopes share proton number Z but differ in neutron number. Stability depends on the neutron-to-proton balance and competition between nuclear attraction and proton repulsion.
Nuclear radius scales approximately as A^(1/3), giving roughly constant nuclear density. Outer electrons control chemical behaviour; the nucleus controls radioactive properties.

sup-0f80619981b08d20-w13:a.ii.hint: Distinguish a prediction for one nucleus from a statistical prediction for a large collection.
notes: Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random: the decay time of one nucleus cannot be predicted, but a large sample follows a statistical decay law.
Alpha, beta and gamma radiation differ in charge, ionization and penetration. Relate the stated observation to the physical property being tested, rather than treating all radiation as identical.

sup-0f80619981b08d20-w13:b.hint: Keep a separate account of nucleon number and electric charge on both sides of the decay.
notes: In alpha decay A decreases by 4 and Z by 2. In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton; in beta-plus decay a proton becomes a neutron, with the appropriate emitted leptons.
Gamma emission changes nuclear energy without changing A or Z. Beta decay shares energy with a neutrino or antineutrino, giving a continuous beta spectrum.

sup-0f80619981b08d20-w13:c.hint: Compare the elapsed time with the half-life, or express the remaining amount as a fraction of the initial amount.
notes: N = N₀e^(−λt), A = λN, and T_half = ln 2/λ. After n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (½)^n.
Subtract background from measured count rates before finding a decay ratio. Activity counts decays per second; it is not the total number of undecayed nuclei.
Link the relevant physical cause to the observation asked about. Naming a law alone does not explain why this particular result follows.

sup-0f80619981b08d20-w14:a.hint: Ask whether the emitted energies form distinct values or a continuous range.
notes: Discrete alpha and gamma energies provide evidence for discrete nuclear levels. A gamma photon carries the difference between levels: E = hf = hc/λ.
Nuclear energy gaps are typically much larger than atomic gaps. A continuous beta spectrum does not disprove nuclear levels because energy is shared with another emitted particle.
